title: Ex Vitro Acclimation and Survival
objective: Explain why in vitro plantlets require a controlled transition to ex vitro humidity, light, airflow, substrate, and microbial conditions.

terms.definition: Outside the in vitro culture vessel, after plant material is transferred to a non-sterile growing environment.
Controlled physiological transition of in vitro plantlets to ex vitro humidity, light, airflow, substrate, and microbial conditions.
Growth using light-driven carbon fixation as the primary carbon source rather than relying on supplied sugar.
The hydrophobic outer layer of aerial plant surfaces that limits uncontrolled water loss and provides a surface barrier.
The ability of stomata to regulate aperture, gas exchange, and transpiration in response to plant and environmental signals.
The proportion of transferred plantlets remaining alive and meeting a defined functional criterion at a stated time after transplant.

coreScience: In vitro plantlets often develop under high humidity, low air movement, limited mechanical load, artificial carbon supply, and low microbial exposure. Leaves and roots formed under those conditions may not immediately regulate water or function like greenhouse-grown tissues.

Acclimatization changes the plant’s atmosphere, substrate, nutrition, irradiance, and microbial environment. Root damage during washing or transfer, poorly aerated media, excessive light, and abrupt humidity reduction can cause losses.

In one drug-type cannabis study, survival differed among hydroponic, peat-plug, and rockwool systems. A newer photoautotrophic study reported direct transplanting without a separate acclimation period for two cultivars under its specific protocol. These findings demonstrate protocol dependence rather than a universal best substrate.
cultivationRelevance: Define transplant readiness, handle roots gently, use a clean but functional substrate, and change humidity and light progressively. Track survival beyond the first upright appearance.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Plantlet size and roots; passage; transfer method; substrate; humidity and venting; light and temperature; irrigation; survival at defined days; new root/shoot growth; losses by cause.

misconceptions: A rooted in vitro shoot is ready for full greenhouse conditions.
The substrate with the highest survival in one paper is universally best.
Standing upright after transfer proves complete acclimation.
evidenceLimits: Acclimation success is genotype-, protocol-, and facility-specific. Survival percentages cannot be transferred without matching the method.
